thread.title: The Dow Tumbles 602 Points Because All the News Looks Bad

title: The Dow Tumbles 602 Points Because All the News Looks Bad
text:
The Dow Tumbles 602 Points Because All the News Looks Bad By Nov. 12, 2018 4:52 p.m. ET Order Reprints Michael Haddad Text size
Not a Good Day. The stock market was pressured on Monday with bad news on multiple fronts. Besides Apple ’s (AAPL) product-demand concerns and a cloud hanging over Goldman Sachs Group (GS), the Trump administration is reportedly looking to broaden its trade battle with China beyond tariffs. All three major indexes ended the day in the red. In today’s After the Bell , we… …contemplate whether we’ve hit the bottom yet in this correction; …wonder what an economic “Cold War” with China could do to the market; …explain how President Donald Trump’s approval rate can affect international stock markets.
Holiday Spending Can’t Offset Trade Concerns
The market is headed into what is usually a positive period: Both the year-end and post-midterm months have traditionally generated some good returns. But that’s not apparent this Monday. Stocks were hammered across the board.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 602.12 points, or 2.32%, to 25,387.18, while the S&P 500 declined 54.79 points, or 1.97%, to 2737.08 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 206.03 points, or 2.78%, to 7200.87.
Maybe the weakness shouldn’t be surprising. The market rebounded a bit last week from October losses, but the internal health of the recent rally hasn’t been impressive, according to Liz Ann Sonders , chief investment strategist at Charles Schwab . Wall Street is now in the longest bull market in history. How did it get there? WSJ's Ken Brown walks us through the record-breaking bull run. Photo illustration: Heather Seidel/The Wall Street Journal
“While stocks were oversold at the late-October lows—and investor sentiment had moved from excessive optimism to pessimism—there wasn’t quite the type of panic selling and investor despair that often serves as a sign of a firm bottom.” This was supported by the low level of the VIX, the CBOE Volatility Index , during the October correction . VIX is usually used as an indicator of the market’s forward-looking volatility.
Fundamentally, the major issues that contributed to the correction—the trade dispute with China, tightening financial conditions, and concerns over the Fed policy—remain in play, according to Sonders, “Little seems actually resolved.” She expects the market to see ongoing bouts of volatility heading into 2019.
The Wall Street Journal reported today that the Trump administration is looking to broaden its battle with China beyond tariffs. Export controls, indictments and other tools might be used to fight the theft of intellectual property. Julian Emanuel from BTIG worries that should the tension with China continue to escalate and the dawn of an economic “Cold War” started to show, the stock market might suffer.
Emanuel writes in a Monday report that U.S. stocks rose 830% in the 29 years from November 1989 to November 2018, while as the prior 29 years–a time of an arms race with the Soviet Union, and the Vietnam War–only saw growth of 564%. “We believe that the lessening of tensions with the U.S.’ rivals in war and peace, the Soviet Union (now Russia) and China was part of the reason such a virtuous economic and investing climate has been possible,” he writes.
The “peace dividend” might be fading this year, however, as the trade war with China intensifies. Although earnings have risen over 20% in 2018, the trailing price/earnings ratio has declined to 19.4 time from 22.3. “Ten years into a global equity bull market, the outcome is less than certain and the potential to ‘roll back time’ to a different, less-profitable era is very real.” writes Emanuel.
The midterm election isn’t helping. “Global stock markets are likely to remain concerned by the trade tensions even though Democrats gained control of the House of Representatives,” writes Schwab’s Sonders, who notes that Congressional approval is not required for the trade tariffs and other actions Trump has implemented. Newsletter Sign-up
However, there are other election-related patterns worth noting. Over the past 25 years, midterm election years usually saw higher international stock markets in November, except for 1994 and 2010 when the U.S. dollar rose 5%, according to Sonders. Although the greenback has been on the rise since the election, another indicator might offer some different insight into the future.
She noted that President Trump’s approval numbers have been a good indicator of U.S. dollar moves since his inauguration, with a delay of about 90 days. “This may be because the approval number captures many things respondents attribute to the President, like the growth of the economy and inflation, which can drive the value of the dollar.” she writes. If this relationship continues to be true, President Trump’s dropping approval rate recently might suggest a weakening dollar, and hence a chance for international stocks to rebound from a tough October.
